DCC-CTX-G1.title: Harborline Support Policy Handbook v4.2
DCC-CTX-G1.text:
Harborline Home Support Policy Handbook - Version 4.2
Effective 1 July 2026. Applies to all Tier 1 phone and chat agents. Supersedes every earlier version.

1. Identity verification
Before discussing any account detail, verify the caller with the full name on the account plus TWO of: (a) the email address on file, (b) the last 4 digits of the card on file, (c) the 6-digit Support PIN shown in the app under Settings > Support. The caller must provide the information; never read it out to them. Account changes (email change, password reset, adding or removing a household member, transferring the subscription) also require the Support PIN or a one-time code sent to the email on file. A caller who is not the account holder can only be helped if they are listed as a household member on the account.

2. Account recovery
If the caller cannot access the email on file and has no Support PIN, open an Account Recovery case using form AR-1. The customer receives a secure upload link for a government photo ID. Trust & Safety reviews AR-1 cases within 3 business days. Agents cannot bypass or speed up AR-1 and must not change the email on file during the call.

3. Password resets
Agents trigger a reset email to the address on file only. The link expires in 30 minutes. Agents never see, set, read out or text a password. Password resets by SMS, or to any new phone number or new email address, are not permitted under any circumstances.

4. Refunds
Hardware: full refund to the original payment method within 30 days of delivery. Opened, non-defective hardware returned within 30 days carries a 15% restocking fee. After 30 days, defective hardware under the 1-year limited warranty is replaced, not refunded.
Subscriptions: monthly Protect and Protect Plus plans are not refunded for partial months. Annual plans cancelled within 14 days of the renewal charge receive a prorated refund; after 14 days the plan runs to the end of the term.
Tier 1 agents may issue refunds up to $150 per case. Anything above $150 needs Tier 2 approval. Refunds post in 5-7 business days.

5. Goodwill credits
Tier 1 agents may apply one goodwill credit of up to $20 per account in any 12-month period, and only for a documented service failure: a cloud outage longer than 4 hours or a missed delivery window. Check the account's credit history before offering anything. Never promise a credit before confirming eligibility. Outage credits for declared incidents are applied automatically on the next bill and do not count toward the goodwill limit.

6. Duplicate charges
Two identical charges within 24 hours: check the billing console. If one is a pending authorization, it drops off on its own within 3-5 business days and no refund is needed. A confirmed duplicate settled charge may be refunded by Tier 1 regardless of the $150 limit.

7. Cancellations
Customers may cancel in the app or by phone. Cancellation takes effect at the end of the current billing period; cameras keep working in free mode (live view only, no recordings). One retention offer may be made per account: 50% off Protect Plus for the next 2 months. If the customer declines, process the cancellation without a second pitch.

8. Shipping
Standard shipping is 3-5 business days; no delivery date is guaranteed. If tracking shows delivered but the customer has nothing, ask them to wait 48 hours, then open a carrier trace. A replacement ships when the trace closes or 7 days after the trace is opened, whichever comes first.

9. Escalation tiers
Tier 1: frontline phone and chat. Tier 2: Senior Support, refunds up to $500, hardware RMAs and unresolved technical faults. Tier 3: Customer Relations (supervisors), complaints about staff, legal or media threats, refunds above $500.
Warm transfers to Tier 2 are available 8am-8pm ET, Monday to Friday. Outside those hours, create an escalation ticket.
A caller who asks for a manager is offered a Tier 3 callback. Supervisors call back within 1 business day. Do not promise a specific time.

10. Response-time targets
Chat: first reply within 2 minutes. Email tickets: first response within 24 hours. Tier 2 escalation tickets: acknowledged within 4 business hours. Callbacks are booked in 2-hour windows, never exact times.

11. Outages
During a declared outage, direct customers to the status page and read only what it says. Do not give an ETA unless the status page shows one.

12. Privacy
Cloud video is kept for 30 days on Protect and 60 days on Protect Plus. Requests to export or delete data go through the Privacy Portal; agents cannot delete recordings on a call. Support staff cannot view live video or recordings.

DCC-CTX-G2.title: Harborline Cam 2 and Home Hub Troubleshooting Guide
DCC-CTX-G2.text:
Harborline Cam 2 and Home Hub - Tier 1 Troubleshooting Guide (rev. 2026-08)

Start every technical call by asking which device, what the status light is doing, and when it last worked.

Status light codes (Cam 2)
- Pulsing blue: pairing mode, waiting for setup in the app.
- Solid blue: connected and recording normally.
- Blinking amber: no Wi-Fi connection.
- Solid amber: connected to Wi-Fi but cannot reach the Harborline cloud.
- Solid red: firmware failure. Do not attempt more than one power cycle; go to Escalation below.
- Flashing white: factory reset in progress.

Camera offline / blinking amber
1. Confirm the router is on and other devices have internet.
2. Cam 2 only connects to 2.4 GHz networks. If the customer recently changed router or split bands, the camera will not see a 5 GHz-only network.
3. Power cycle: unplug for 10 seconds, plug back in, wait 2 minutes.
4. Move the camera or router closer; a signal below 2 bars in the app causes dropouts.
5. If still offline, factory reset (below) and set up again.

Factory reset
Hold the reset button on the back for 15 seconds until the light flashes white. The camera loses its settings and motion zones and must be added again in the app. Recordings already in the cloud are not deleted.

App login loop
If the app returns to the login screen after signing in: update the app to version 6.3 or later (older versions have a known token bug), then clear the app cache (Android: Settings > Apps > Harborline > Storage; iOS: offload and reinstall the app). If two-step codes do not arrive, check the email on file, not SMS; Harborline two-step codes are sent by email only.

Motion alerts not arriving
Check phone notification permissions for the app, check that the camera is not in Privacy Mode, and check that the motion zone covers the area. Sensitivity below 3 misses people at a distance.

Live view buffering
Each Cam 2 needs at least 2 Mbps of upload. Ask the customer to run a speed test near the camera. Lower live view quality to Standard as a workaround.

Home Hub error codes
- E-14: the Hub's SD card is full; local recording stops until it is cleared in the app.
- E-22: the Hub cannot reach the cloud; treat like solid amber.
- E-31: the Hub is overheating; move it out of enclosed cabinets.

Escalation
Escalate to Tier 2 for an RMA when the light is solid red, a factory reset has failed twice, or the device is physically damaged. Never promise a replacement yourself; Tier 2 confirms warranty and ships the RMA. Do not ask customers to open the device.

Effective 1 March 2024. Check the Knowledge Base for the current version before relying on this document.

Verification
Verify callers with their date of birth and billing ZIP code before discussing the account.

Refunds

DLEC-CTX-G1.title: ECON 214 Week 6 slides - Price elasticity of demand
DLEC-CTX-G1.text:
ECON 214 - Intermediate Microeconomics
Week 6 Lecture Slides: Price Elasticity of Demand
Prof. Adaeze Okonkwo-Hale | Harlow State University | Section 002

Slide 1 - Learning goals
- Compute own-price elasticity of demand using the course's midpoint convention
- Classify demand as elastic, inelastic, or unit elastic
- Connect elasticity to what happens to total revenue when price changes

Slide 2 - Definition
Own-price elasticity of demand measures how responsive quantity demanded is to a change in the good's own price:
E = (% change in quantity demanded) / (% change in price)
Because demand slopes down, the raw ratio is negative.

Slide 3 - ECON 214 convention (read this carefully)
In this course we ALWAYS use the midpoint (arc) formula unless a question explicitly says "point elasticity":
% change in Q = (Q2 - Q1) / ((Q1 + Q2) / 2)
% change in P = (P2 - P1) / ((P1 + P2) / 2)
We report own-price elasticity as an absolute value, rounded to two decimals. So you write 1.22, not -1.22.
Many textbooks (including the optional Marchetti text) divide by the starting values instead. That gives a different number for the same data, and it gives a different number depending on whether the price goes up or down. The midpoint version gives the same answer in both directions, which is why we use it.

Slide 4 - Classification (using the absolute value |E|)
- |E| > 1: elastic
- |E| < 1: inelastic
- |E| = 1 exactly: unit elastic
Note: 1.00 after rounding counts as unit elastic on problem sets and exams.

Slide 5 - Worked example: the Quad coffee cart
The coffee cart outside Benning Hall raises the price of a small drip coffee from $3.00 to $3.60. Daily sales fall from 500 cups to 400 cups.
Step 1: % change in Q = (400 - 500) / 450 = -0.2222, i.e. -22.2%
Step 2: % change in P = (3.60 - 3.00) / 3.30 = 0.1818, i.e. 18.2%
Step 3: E = -22.2% / 18.2% = -1.22
Step 4: report |E| = 1.22, so demand is elastic over this range.
Check: with the starting-value method you would get -20% / 20% = -1.00 and call it unit elastic. Same data, different classification. This is exactly why we fix one convention.

Slide 6 - Elasticity and total revenue
Total revenue TR = P x Q.
Before: $3.00 x 500 = $1,500 per day. After: $3.60 x 400 = $1,440 per day.
Rule: when demand is elastic, a price increase lowers total revenue; when demand is inelastic, a price increase raises total revenue; at unit elasticity total revenue does not change.
The coffee cart is consistent with the rule: elastic demand, price went up, revenue fell by $60 a day.

Slide 7 - What makes demand more elastic?
- Close substitutes are available (the dining hall sells drip coffee for $2.25)
- The good is a larger share of the budget
- A longer time horizon to adjust
- A narrowly defined market ("drip coffee at this cart" versus "caffeine")

Slide 8 - Exam notes
- Midterm 2 covers Weeks 5 to 8. Elasticity questions on Midterm 2 must use the midpoint formula; answers that use starting values get at most half credit.
- Show all four steps from Slide 5.
- The elasticity formula sheet is NOT provided on Midterm 2. Memorize the formulas.

Slide 9 - Preview of Week 7
Cross-price elasticity: the sign matters there (positive means substitutes, negative means complements), so we do NOT take absolute values for cross-price elasticity.

DLEC-CTX-G2.title: CS 261 Lecture 11 notes - Binary heaps and build-heap
DLEC-CTX-G2.text:
CS 261 - Data Structures
Lecture 11 Notes: Binary Heaps and Build-Heap
Prof. Tomasz Reinholt-Vega | Carrow Institute of Technology

1. What a binary heap is
A binary heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array that satisfies the heap-order property. In CS 261 we use MIN-heaps by default: every node's key is less than or equal to the keys of its children, so the smallest key sits at the root.

2. CS 261 array convention (differs from the 0-indexed code you will see online)
We store the heap 1-indexed. Index 0 is left empty (we write it as _).
- parent(i) = floor(i / 2)
- left(i) = 2i
- right(i) = 2i + 1
If you see parent(i) = floor((i - 1) / 2) and left(i) = 2i + 1 online, that is the 0-indexed layout. Both are correct for their own layout, but on CS 261 quizzes you must use the 1-indexed formulas.

3. Height convention
In CS 261 the height of a tree counts NODES on the longest root-to-leaf path, so a single node has height 1 and an empty tree has height 0. (Most textbooks count edges, so for them a single node has height 0.) With our convention a heap with n keys has height floor(log2 n) + 1. Example: n = 7 gives height 3.

4. Sift-down (heapify at index i)
Compare the key at i with its children. If the smaller child is smaller than the key at i, swap with that smaller child and repeat from the child's index. Stop when the key is no larger than both children or when i has no children. Cost: O(height).

5. Build-heap (bottom-up)
Call sift-down on i = floor(n / 2), floor(n / 2) - 1, ..., 1. Leaves (indices greater than floor(n / 2)) are already heaps, so we skip them.
Total cost is O(n), not O(n log n). Most nodes live near the bottom and can only sift down a short distance; the sum of heights over all nodes is bounded by a linear function of n.

6. Worked example (show the array after every sift-down call; this is required on quizzes)
Input, n = 7: [_, 9, 4, 7, 1, 8, 2, 6]
Start at i = floor(7 / 2) = 3.
- sift-down(3): 7 vs children 2 (i=6) and 6 (i=7). Swap with 2. Array: [_, 9, 4, 2, 1, 8, 7, 6]
- sift-down(2): 4 vs children 1 (i=4) and 8 (i=5). Swap with 1. Index 4 has no children. Array: [_, 9, 1, 2, 4, 8, 7, 6]
- sift-down(1): 9 vs children 1 (i=2) and 2 (i=3). Swap with 1. Continue at i=2: 9 vs children 4 (i=4) and 8 (i=5). Swap with 4. Index 4 has no children. Array: [_, 1, 4, 2, 9, 8, 7, 6]
Result: [_, 1, 4, 2, 9, 8, 7, 6]. Four swaps total.

7. Other operations
- peek-min: O(1), it is A[1].
- insert: put the key at A[n + 1], then sift-up. O(log n).
- extract-min: move A[n] to A[1], shrink the heap, sift-down(1). O(log n).
- Finding the MAXIMUM in a min-heap is not cheap: the max is somewhere among the leaves, so it takes O(n) in general.

8. Logistics
Quiz 4 (next Thursday) covers heaps: sift-down traces, build-heap traces, and the index formulas above. Traces must use the 1-indexed layout. Priority queues and heapsort are on Quiz 5, not Quiz 4.

DLEC-CTX-C1.title: ECON 214 TA recitation handout - Elasticity quick guide
DLEC-CTX-C1.text:
ECON 214 Recitation Handout - Week 6
Elasticity Quick Guide
Prepared by TA Marcus Delacroix-Byrne for the Friday recitation sections

Formula
Own-price elasticity of demand = % change in quantity demanded / % change in price, where each percentage change is computed from the ORIGINAL value:
% change in Q = (Q2 - Q1) / Q1
% change in P = (P2 - P1) / P1
Keep the negative sign. A demand elasticity of -1.5 should be written as -1.5 so the grader can see you know demand slopes down.

Classification
- E below -1 (for example -1.5): elastic
- E between -1 and 0: inelastic
- E equal to -1: for this course, treat unit elastic as elastic, since the revenue logic is the same.

Practice example: the Quad coffee cart
The cart raises the price of a small drip coffee from $3.00 to $3.60 and daily sales fall from 500 to 400 cups.
% change in Q = -100 / 500 = -20%
% change in P = 0.60 / 3.00 = 20%
E = -20% / 20% = -1.00, so demand here is elastic (unit elastic counts as elastic).

Total revenue
Revenue before: $1,500 per day. Revenue after: $1,440 per day. Because the cart is on the elastic side, revenue moves in the opposite direction from price.

Exam tips
- On Midterm 2 either the original-value method or the midpoint method gets full credit, so use whichever is faster for you.
- A formula sheet will be stapled to the back of Midterm 2, so you do not need to memorize the formulas.
- Cross-price elasticity: take the absolute value, same as own-price, and report it to two decimals.
- If a question does not say which price is the starting price, use the lower price as the base.

Office hours for recitation questions: Fridays 1-2 pm, Econ Commons table 4.

DJOB-CTX-G1.title: Dockhand project write-up (portfolio notes)
DJOB-CTX-G1.text:
DOCKHAND - PROJECT WRITE-UP
Portfolio notes, Tobias Venkataraman (personal notes, not a Larkspur Freight document)
Last edited: August 2026

WHAT IT IS
Dockhand is the Kafka event pipeline that carries shipment status events (picked up, in transit, delayed, delivered, exception) from the carrier-facing services at Larkspur Freight to everything downstream: customer tracking pages, billing, and the nightly reconciliation job. It processes about 2.3 million shipment status events per day. At the weekday 7 a.m. Eastern dispatch peak it sustains roughly 610 events per second.

WHY WE BUILT IT
Before Dockhand, each carrier integration wrote status updates straight into PostgreSQL and then made a separate HTTP call to notify downstream services. If the process died between the database commit and the HTTP call, downstream systems never heard about the update; if the call was retried after a timeout, they heard about it twice. Billing saw duplicate "delivered" events often enough that finance kept a manual spreadsheet of corrections.

DESIGN
- Transactional outbox. The service that records a status change inserts a row into a shipment_outbox table in the same PostgreSQL transaction as the status update itself. Either both commit or neither does.
- Relay. A small Go relay polls shipment_outbox every 200 ms, claims up to 500 unpublished rows with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, publishes them to Kafka, and marks them published. Several relay instances can run at once without stepping on each other.
- Topic layout. One topic, shipment.status.v1, with 24 partitions keyed by load ID, so all events for a given load stay in order.
- Consumer-side dedupe. The relay is at-least-once, so each consumer records the event_id in a processed_events table inside the same transaction as its own write, and skips IDs it has already seen. processed_events rows are kept for 14 days.
- The few consumers that call external carrier APIs reuse the idempotency-key approach from my open-source library, Sparrowhawk.

ROLLOUT
I wrote the design doc in November 2023 and built Dockhand with one other engineer, Renata Obi. We ran it in shadow mode for 3 weeks, comparing its output against the old HTTP notifications, and cut over carrier by carrier, finishing in February 2024. Duplicate "delivered" events reaching billing went to zero in the first full month after cutover, and finance retired the correction spreadsheet.

THE INCIDENT
In October 2024 the relay fell 38 minutes behind during the morning peak. Customer tracking pages showed stale statuses and support received about 70 tickets before we caught up. Root cause: the hourly job that prunes published rows from shipment_outbox had been disabled during an unrelated migration and never re-enabled, so the table had grown to about 40 million rows and the relay's "find unpublished rows" query had degraded into a large scan. I was the on-call engineer that morning.

Fixes: a partial index on shipment_outbox covering only unpublished rows; re-enabling the prune job with a check that alerts if it has not run in 3 hours; and a Datadog monitor on relay lag that pages at 5 minutes instead of relying on customer reports. I wrote the postmortem and turned the recovery steps into one of the team's incident runbooks.

WHAT I WOULD DO DIFFERENTLY
- Alert on outbox table size and relay lag from day one, not after the first incident.
- Evaluate change data capture (for example, reading the PostgreSQL write-ahead log) instead of polling. We chose polling for simplicity and it has held up, but it adds query load on the primary.
- Write the consumer dedupe contract down earlier; two teams initially implemented it slightly differently.

DSEM-CTX-G1.title: Thesis chapter 5: STAGE-KD keyword spotting results
DSEM-CTX-G1.text:
Chapter 5: Results and Discussion
Thesis: Staged Knowledge Distillation for Always-On Keyword Spotting on Microcontrollers
Candidate: R. Okonkwo-Hale, Department of Electrical Engineering, Veldmoor University (examination copy, final version)

5.1 Experimental setup
The teacher network, KWS-Large, has 18.4M parameters. The student, KWS-Tiny, has 212k parameters and is the model deployed on device. All models were trained on the Corvid Commands v2 corpus: 41,300 one-second utterances covering 35 keywords from 1,912 speakers. The test split contains 6,120 utterances from 288 held-out speakers who do not appear in training or validation.

We compare three ways of training KWS-Tiny: (a) training from scratch with cross-entropy, (b) standard KD, i.e. single-stage logit matching with temperature 4, and (c) STAGE-KD, our three-stage method. STAGE-KD runs logit matching first, then aligns intermediate features at student layers 3 and 6 with teacher layers 8 and 16, and finally fine-tunes for 2 epochs on hard labels with label smoothing of 0.1. Every configuration in Table 5.1 was trained with 5 random seeds; we report mean and standard deviation.

On-device numbers were measured on an Arlo M4 development board running at 80 MHz. Latency is measured per 1-second window, from feature input to posterior output; front-end feature extraction (40-band log-mel) was not timed separately.

5.2 Main results
Table 5.1 (test accuracy, mean +/- s.d. over 5 seeds):
- Scratch: 89.7% +/- 0.6
- Standard KD: 91.8% +/- 0.4
- STAGE-KD: 93.2% +/- 0.3
- Teacher (KWS-Large, reference only): 95.9%

STAGE-KD closes roughly a third of the gap between standard KD and the teacher. At the operating point of 1 false accept per hour, the false reject rate is 6.8% for STAGE-KD versus 9.4% for standard KD.

On the Arlo M4, KWS-Tiny runs in 14.2 ms per window with a peak RAM of 96 KB. Because all three training methods produce the same architecture, latency and memory are identical across them. We report latency only; energy per inference was not measured, as the board lacks a current-sense header.

5.3 Significance
We compared STAGE-KD against standard KD with a paired bootstrap over test utterances (10,000 resamples), pooling the predictions of the five seeds. We chose this over a t-test across seeds because five seeds give too few samples for a seed-level test to be informative. The difference is significant (p < 0.01). The bootstrap tests were not corrected for multiple comparisons across the ablation variants.

5.4 Ablations
Ablations used 3 seeds only, due to compute limits. Removing stage 2 (feature alignment) lowers accuracy to 92.0%; removing stage 3 (hard-label fine-tuning) lowers it to 92.9%. We read this as stage 2 contributing most of the gain, but the ablation differences are small relative to seed variance and should be treated as indicative.

5.5 Noise robustness
Under babble noise at 0 dB SNR, STAGE-KD reaches 71.5% and standard KD 70.9%. This gap is within seed variance, and we make no claim that STAGE-KD improves noise robustness.

5.6 Limitations
- English only; 71% of speakers self-reported US English, so accent coverage is skewed.
- One microcontroller (Arlo M4); results may not transfer to other boards or clock speeds.
- No energy measurements; latency is used as a proxy for cost.
- Near-field recordings only; nothing was tested beyond 1.5 m.
- Five seeds limit how precisely we can estimate variance, and the ablations use three.
- Baselines are limited to scratch training and standard KD.

5.7 Summary
STAGE-KD improves a 212k-parameter keyword spotter by 1.4 points over standard KD at no on-device cost, because the deployed architecture is unchanged. Future work: multilingual data, energy profiling, and far-field evaluation.

DSEM-CTX-G2.title: Research summary: SMS reminders and clinic attendance, Marlow District pilot
DSEM-CTX-G2.text:
Research Summary: Timed SMS Reminders and Outpatient Attendance
Marlow District Pilot, 2025 - summary prepared for the Health Services Research seminar
Authors: T. Brannigan (presenting), A. Idowu, M. Castellanos-Reyes

Background
Missed outpatient appointments in Marlow District ran at roughly 28% in 2024. We tested whether two timed text reminders improve attendance.

Design
Cluster-randomised trial across 14 clinics: 7 intervention, 7 control. Clinics volunteered in response to a district-wide invitation; of the 31 district clinics invited, 14 agreed. Randomisation was at clinic level, stratified by clinic size. Over a 12-week period the trial covered 2,406 scheduled appointments among 1,184 patients (1,221 appointments in intervention clinics, 1,185 in control clinics). Clinic staff and patients were not blinded to allocation.

Intervention clinics sent an SMS reminder 48 hours before the appointment and a second SMS 3 hours before. Control clinics continued usual practice (no reminder). Both reminders were always sent together, so the design cannot separate the effect of the 48-hour reminder from the 3-hour reminder.

Outcomes and analysis
The primary outcome was attendance at the scheduled appointment. The secondary outcome was late cancellation (less than 24 hours notice). Clinical health outcomes were not measured.

Analysis was intention-to-treat using mixed-effects logistic regression with a clinic random intercept, adjusting for age band, sex and appointment type. We used a random intercept because appointments within the same clinic are correlated; a simple chi-square test would treat all 2,406 appointments as independent and overstate precision. Appointments with a missing outcome (3.2%) were excluded (complete-case analysis).

Results
- Attendance: 78.4% in intervention clinics versus 71.9% in control clinics.
- Adjusted odds ratio 1.41 (95% CI 1.12 to 1.77).
- Late cancellations fell from 9.3% (control) to 7.1% (intervention).
- Patients aged 65 and over: OR 1.09 (95% CI 0.81 to 1.47), not significant. This subgroup contributed 412 appointments, and the trial was not powered for subgroup analysis.
- Delivery: 5,120 messages were sent; 6% were undeliverable (invalid or inactive numbers).
- Cost: each SMS cost 0.04 per message under the district's bulk contract.

Interpretation
Two timed reminders were associated with a 6.5 percentage point increase in attendance. Because only 14 clinics were randomised, the confidence interval is wide despite the number of appointments. The weaker estimate in older patients may reflect lower mobile phone use or simply the small subgroup; the data cannot distinguish these.

Limitations
- Short follow-up: 12-week duration, so we cannot say whether the effect persists or fades.
- Volunteer clinics may be more organised or motivated than those that declined.
- No blinding of clinic staff.
- 6% of messages were undeliverable and phone number accuracy was not audited.
- Results were not stratified by income or employment.
- We did not conduct a cost-effectiveness analysis.

Next steps
A follow-on trial would randomise from all 31 district clinics, run for 12 months, and test the 48-hour and 3-hour reminders as separate arms.

DSEM-CTX-G3.title: Slide deck: microplastics in Brenn River mussels
DSEM-CTX-G3.text:
Slide deck: Microplastic Loads in Freshwater Mussels, Brenn River Catchment
Presenter: J. Saelens, MSc Environmental Science, Harrowgate College. Seminar version, 12 slides.

Slide 1 - Title
Microplastic loads in freshwater mussels upstream and downstream of the Kessel wastewater treatment plant.

Slide 2 - Question
Do mussels downstream of the Kessel plant carry more microplastic particles than mussels upstream?

Slide 3 - Sites and sampling
6 sites: 3 upstream and 3 downstream of the plant outfall, each 0.5 to 4 km from the outfall. 240 mussels in total, 40 per site, collected by hand in a single sampling season (August 2025). Shell length ranged from 52-88 mm.

Slide 4 - Lab method
Soft tissue digested in 10% KOH at 40 C for 48 h. Filtrate stained with Nile red and particles counted under fluorescence microscopy. Lower size cutoff: 50 um; smaller particles, including nanoplastics, were not detected.

Slide 5 - Quality control
Procedural blanks run with every batch of 10 samples; mean 0.6 particles per blank, subtracted from sample counts. Cotton lab coats, filtered water, covered glassware.

Slide 6 - Polymer confirmation
A random 15% of counted particles were analysed by micro-FTIR. 81% of the analysed particles were confirmed as synthetic polymers; the rest were mostly cellulose or protein. Polyester was the most common polymer (38% of confirmed particles), followed by polypropylene (22%).

Slide 7 - Results: particles per individual
Upstream mean: 3.8 particles per individual. Downstream mean: 7.1 particles per individual.

Slide 8 - Results: particles per gram
Upstream: 0.42 particles per gram wet tissue. Downstream: 0.83 particles per gram wet tissue.

Slide 9 - Particle shape
Fibres made up 64% of particles, fragments 29%, films and beads the rest.

Slide 10 - Statistics
Kruskal-Wallis test across the 6 sites: H = 21.4, p < 0.001. Dunn post hoc tests: each downstream site differed from each upstream site; no difference among sites on the same side of the outfall. We used a rank-based test because counts were strongly right-skewed and zero-inflated.

Slide 11 - Limitations
- One season only; no winter or spring sampling.
- No water or sediment samples taken at the same time, so we cannot say where the particles come from within the river.
- Nile red can stain some natural organic matter; FTIR on a 15% subset mitigates but does not remove false positives.
- Mussel size varied (52-88 mm) and was not fully adjusted for in the analysis.
- We did not have access to plant discharge records, so counts could not be related to effluent volume.
- Human consumption risk was not assessed; these are not a commercially harvested population.

Slide 12 - Conclusion
Downstream mussels carried roughly double the microplastic load of upstream mussels, by count and by tissue weight. Recommend repeat sampling across seasons with paired water samples.

Version 1.3 - owner Hiro Tanaka (PM) - last updated Friday 18 September 2026
Change log: v1.3 moves CSV export to 2.5 and records the Kestrel Messaging choice (both from the 17 September sync).

Goal
Release 2.4 makes Orchard usable for hourly teams who do not sit at a desk: shift reminders by SMS, clock-in that works without signal, and a clear pay-period summary.

In scope for 2.4
1. Shift reminders by SMS (Kestrel Messaging), opt-in per worker.
2. Offline clock-in behind feature flag offline_clockin_v1.
3. Pay-period summary screen (needs Ledger API v5).
4. Accessibility fixes to WCAG 2.2 AA on 14 screens.

Out of scope for 2.4
- CSV export of timesheets (moved to 2.5)
- Dark mode (2.6)
- Manager approval flow redesign (2.6)
- Apple Watch app (not planned)

Milestones
- Tue 29 Sep: pay-period endpoints migrated to Ledger v5 (Priya Nand)
- Fri 2 Oct: Platform ships Ledger API v5 bulk endpoints (external; owner Rafael Duarte)
- Mon 5 Oct: go/no-go on the Ledger fallback (Hiro Tanaka and Lena Okafor)
- Fri 9 Oct: code freeze
- Wed 14 Oct: beta to 400 pilot users across three customers: Brennan Foods (Ohio), Tidewater Clinics (Halifax, Canada), Marlow Transit (Oregon)
- Wed 28 Oct: GA, phased release over 7 days on both stores
- Wed 11 Nov: 2.5 planning kickoff

Dependencies
- Ledger API v5 bulk endpoints (Platform team). Needed by the pay-period summary.
- Kestrel Messaging contract (Procurement). Monthly SMS spend above $5,000 needs Finance sign-off; the current estimate is 1.2 million messages a month, about $8,500.
- Kestrel carrier registration for Canadian numbers takes up to 10 business days after the contract is signed. It is required before any Tidewater Clinics worker can receive SMS reminders.
- App store review: keep 3 business days of buffer before GA.

Risks and mitigations
R1. Ledger API v5 bulk endpoints slip past 2 October. Impact: the pay-period summary screen cannot load totals for pay periods longer than 14 days. Mitigation: fall back to the v4 read endpoints for 2.4 and show a "totals updating" state. The call is made at the 5 October go/no-go. If we fall back, the pay-period summary ships read-only.
R2. SMS deliverability in Canada if carrier registration is late. Mitigation: sign the contract by 1 October; reminders for Tidewater default to email until registration completes.
R3. QA capacity. Tomas Reyes is shared with the Web team until 5 October. Mitigation: a QA contractor for 2 weeks starting 5 October (budget approved by Lena Okafor).
R4. Offline clock-in data conflicts. Mitigation: the flag stays at 10% of beta users; full rollout only after conflict resolution passes regression.

Roles
- Accountable: Hiro Tanaka
- Engineering lead: Lena Okafor
- Backend: Priya Nand. Mobile: Marcus Oyelaran. Design: Dana Whitfield. QA: Tomas Reyes.

Success measures for beta
- Reminder opt-in: at least 40% of pilot workers
- Clock-in failures: under 0.5% of attempts
- Crash-free sessions: target to be agreed (see the 17 September sync)

Communication
Hiro owns all customer-facing communication about dates and scope. Engineers do not give dates to pilot customers directly.

DTECH-CTX-G1.title: Quarrystone take-home: Pager Quiet Windows (problem statement)
DTECH-CTX-G1.text:
QUARRYSTONE ANALYTICS - PLATFORM TEAM TAKE-HOME (v3)
Problem: Pager Quiet Windows

Background
Our on-call tool lets engineers schedule "quiet windows" during which non-critical pages for a host are held back. Engineers create windows independently, so the list for one host arrives unsorted and often overlapping. Before we push windows to the pager we collapse them into the smallest equivalent list.

Part 1: merge_windows(windows, grace)
Input:
- windows: a list of pairs [start, end], in integer minutes since the start of the quarter. A window covers minute start (inclusive) up to end (exclusive), so [10, 20] covers 10 minutes.
- grace: an integer number of minutes.

Rules:
1. If any window has end < start, raise ValueError with the message "inverted window at index i", where i is the index of the FIRST such window in the input list as given (before any sorting).
2. A window with end == start covers no time and is dropped silently. A dropped window must not bridge two other windows.
3. After sorting by start, a window merges into the current merged window when its start <= current end + grace. Windows that touch (next start == current end) therefore always merge, even with grace 0.
4. Grace only decides whether two windows merge; it never extends a window. A merged window ends at the largest end among the windows it absorbed.
5. Return the merged windows sorted by start, as a new list of [start, end] pairs. Do not mutate the input list or the pairs inside it.

Examples
Example 1: windows = [[10, 20], [15, 30], [40, 50]], grace = 0
Output: [[10, 30], [40, 50]]

Example 2: windows = [[5, 10], [10, 12], [13, 20]], grace = 0
Output: [[5, 12], [13, 20]]
([5, 10] and [10, 12] touch, so they merge. The gap from 12 to 13 is 1 minute, which is larger than grace 0.)

Example 3: windows = [[5, 10], [10, 12], [13, 20]], grace = 1
Output: [[5, 20]]
(Note the result is [5, 20], not [5, 21]: grace never extends a window.)

Example 4: windows = [[30, 30], [1, 4], [2, 3]], grace = 5
Output: [[1, 4]]
([30, 30] is dropped; [2, 3] lies inside [1, 4].)

Example 5: windows = [[0, 10], [11, 11], [12, 20]], grace = 1
Output: [[0, 10], [12, 20]]
([11, 11] is dropped before merging, so it cannot bridge the gap between 10 and 12.)

Example 6: windows = [[7, 3], [1, 2], [9, 4]], grace = 0
Raises ValueError("inverted window at index 0")

Example 7: windows = [], grace = 10
Output: []

Part 2: total_quiet_minutes(windows, grace)
Return the total number of minutes covered by the output of merge_windows. A gap that grace bridged is counted, because the merged window spans it. For Example 1 the answer is 30, for Example 3 it is 15, and for Example 7 it is 0.

Constraints
- 0 <= len(windows) <= 200,000
- 0 <= start, end <= 10^9
- 0 <= grace <= 60
- Your solution must run in O(n log n) time. Our reference solution runs in under 1 second in Python for n = 200,000.
- Python 3.10+ or Go 1.22+. Standard library only.

What we look at
Correctness on our hidden cases (including every edge case above), readability, the tests you write yourself, and a short note (under 200 words) explaining your approach and its complexity. Please do not spend more than 3 hours.

Live follow-up
In the follow-up interview we will ask how your design changes if windows arrive one at a time from a stream and the pager needs to ask "is minute t quiet?" at any moment.

DTECH-CTX-G2.title: Lanternfish design notes and retrospective
DTECH-CTX-G2.text:
LANTERNFISH - DESIGN NOTES AND RETROSPECTIVE
Author: Dashiell Marrow, SRE I, Cindervale Systems. Written December 2025 for the SRE team wiki.

Problem
The checkout path (cart-api -> pricing -> payments-gateway) had a p99 of about 1,380 ms against an SLO target of 900 ms. Traces showed unexplained gaps before outbound calls that no span covered. We suspected DNS but had no per-pod data. CoreDNS exposes metrics per CoreDNS replica, only for the queries that reach it, and it sees a client's search-domain expansion as several unrelated queries rather than one slow lookup.

Design
Lanternfish is a Rust sidecar built on the tokio async runtime, using the hickory-proto crate to parse DNS messages. It is injected into pods on the checkout path.
- The pod uses dnsPolicy None with a dnsConfig whose first nameserver is 127.0.0.1. Lanternfish listens on 127.0.0.1:53 over UDP; only the sidecar container gets the NET_BIND_SERVICE capability.
- Each query is forwarded unchanged to the cluster DNS service IP. Lanternfish times the lookup from the moment the query arrives from the application to the moment the response is written back.
- It exports a Prometheus histogram, lanternfish_lookup_seconds, with 12 buckets from 1 ms to 2.5 s and the labels qtype, rcode and upstream. The queried name is deliberately NOT a label, to keep cardinality bounded.
- A counter, lanternfish_search_expansions_total, counts queries for names that end in one of the pod's search suffixes and come back NXDOMAIN.
- The existing Prometheus scrapes it every 15 seconds; no new storage was needed.
- The second nameserver line in dnsConfig points straight at the cluster DNS IP, with options timeout:1, so a crashed sidecar costs a one-second retry rather than an outage.

Why a sidecar
We considered three options:
1. CoreDNS metrics. Already existed, but aggregated per replica rather than per pod, and blind to how many expansions one application lookup triggered.
2. An eBPF probe on each node. Per-pod data without touching pods, but our GKE nodes ran Container-Optimized OS, nobody on the team had written eBPF before, and we estimated 4 to 6 weeks.
3. A sidecar. Per pod by construction, easy to remove, and about 2 weeks of work.
We chose the sidecar. The trade-off: it only sees pods it is injected into, and it adds one local hop to every lookup.

Rollout
Lanternfish ran on the 14 deployments of the checkout path for three weeks.

Findings
- 31% of p99 latency on the checkout path came from DNS resolution.
- The main cause was the default ndots:5. External names such as the payment processor's API have fewer than five dots, so the resolver tried every search domain first. On GKE that meant up to 10 failed queries (A and AAAA for each of 5 search domains) before the real lookup.
- A smaller share came from occasional 5-second stalls caused by a known conntrack race when A and AAAA queries go out in parallel over UDP.

Fix
- Priya Oduya (senior SRE) reviewed the design and ran the rollout of the fix; I wrote the sidecar, the dashboards and the analysis.
- Checkout-path pods moved to ndots:2, and the three external payment endpoints were changed to fully qualified names with a trailing dot.
- NodeLocal DNSCache was enabled on the cluster, which also removed the conntrack stalls.
- Checkout p99 fell from 1,380 ms to 910 ms, and DNS dropped to about 6% of p99.

Overhead and limitations
- Median added latency is about 0.3 ms per lookup; each sidecar uses about 6 MiB of memory and under 5 millicores of CPU.
- UDP only: queries that fall back to TCP after a truncated response are passed through and not measured.
- After the fix we removed the sidecar from 9 of the 14 deployments and kept it on 5 as a canary.
- It was never deployed to the other two clusters, and it has not been open-sourced.

DTECH-CTX-C1.title: Quarrystone take-home candidate FAQ
DTECH-CTX-C1.text:
QUARRYSTONE TAKE-HOME - CANDIDATE FAQ
Forwarded by Pilar Okonkwo-Reyes, Technical Recruiter. Compiled from questions earlier candidates asked about the Pager Quiet Windows exercise. Different interviewers wrote different answers.

Q: How long should I spend on it?
A: Please keep it under 3 hours. We are not grading polish.

Q: How big are the inputs?
A: Each host has at most 200,000 windows, so an O(n log n) sort-based solution is what we expect.

Q: Do windows that touch, like [5, 10] and [10, 12], merge when grace is 0?
A: No. Ends are exclusive, so [5, 10] and [10, 12] stay separate unless grace is at least 1.

Q: What languages can I use?
A: Python 3.10+ or Go 1.22+, standard library only.

Q: Can I use sortedcontainers or another package for part 2?
A: Yes, any package on PyPI is fine as long as you pin it in requirements.txt.

Q: What does the grader check first?
A: The edge cases. Touching windows always merge, even with grace 0, and zero-length windows are dropped. Most failed submissions get one of those wrong.

Q: What is the performance bar?
A: The hidden cases go up to 2 million windows per host, and the reference solution finishes in under 1 second in Python. If yours takes a few seconds that is fine; we cut off at 5 seconds.

Q: When is it due?
A: You have 48 hours from when the link opens. Most people spend a full day on it.

Q: Should part 2 count grace gaps as quiet time?
A: No, only minutes actually inside a window count.
DTECH-CTX-C1.notes: Contradictions: touching windows "stay separate" vs "always merge" at grace 0; max input 200,000 vs 2 million windows per host; "standard library only" vs "any package on PyPI is fine"; "under 3 hours" vs "48 hours / most people spend a full day"; part 2 says grace gaps are not counted, which clashes with merged windows spanning them; 1 s reference vs 5 s cutoff for an input 10x the stated max.
